segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I've had a bunch of bike accidents in the last year and a half. And the moment that things go wrong is always the same. These accidents happen during my morning commute. And they always happen when it rains.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I have this very light bicycle I got. And when it rains, something about this bike on the city streets-- a metal grate, a slippery patch of any sort at all, can make the bike slip out from under me. I have broken a clavicle. I banged up my wrist. I've given myself some kind of bruise on my right arm that still wakes me up at night, months later.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And in each of these three accidents-- you know, like, when you're falling, there's that second or two when you realize you're going down, and you're on your way down, but you haven't actually hit the ground yet? Weirdly, it is enough time for a bunch of thoughts to go through your head. And all three times, like I say, it's been the same. Somehow I get very calm and I think, oh, this isn't going to be so bad. I'm not going very fast. The ground isn't that far. Is a car coming? OK, no car is coming. I figured out how to fall. It's going to be fine-- this time.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I think everybody knows how a person reacts under duress, it can tell you something about them. And I think what this set of thoughts says about me is I am optimistic even when there is no factual basis for it at all. Like, at the exact moment when I'm going to collide with the wet surface of the street, a moment when things are definitely not going to be fine, I'm thinking, things will be fine.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I think this optimism has kept me in faltering relationships. When I mentioned all this at our radio show story meeting this week, one of my coworkers, somebody who I've worked with closely for years, told me-- he has never said this-- that he thinks my optimism is the single most important quality I have. He said he'll tell me there are 17 things that can go wrong with some plan that we have. And I'll just go, eh, let's go for it. Though I have to say, after three accidents, I have learned not to ride this particular bike in the rain. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our program, we have stories where things go very, very badly for people. They are on the way down and in that moment of crisis. What they're thinking reveals so much about who they are. Some people, it leads to new insights. Some, it leads to no insights at all. And some are hit with a lightning bolt of inspiration and figure out how to save themselves. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, "Pirates of the Cari-BEAN-TOWN." One summer, a while back, a group of friends got in trouble, got in over their heads, almost literally, in the middle of Boston Harbor. Our producer, Ike Sriskandarajah, tells the tale-- though, for the purposes of today's story, call him Ishmael.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I've been friends with you this whole time and I didn't know that this is your most told story.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: Well, I wouldn't tell it to you. You were there.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I was there. It was over 10 years ago and I was a new resident in the Boston area. My good friend, Sophie Tintori, introduced me to some people she knew well. We liked the same kinds of jokes and could only afford the same kind of rent. So we moved into a big house together. And soon, we got to the stage in any relationship where someone suggests taking things to the next level.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: So I don't know exactly how it came up, but maybe eight friends or so decided to go in, collectively, and buy a used boat. And to my understanding, none of them knew a single thing about boats.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: True. But did you know the word "catamaran" comes from Tamil? Kattu maram, "wood tied together." Those are my guys. So that's one thing I know about boats. And maybe more ancestral knowledge was just waiting to surface if I owned a boat.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Here's how it happened. Our friend Max brought us the opportunity. He knew a person who knew a person who needed to get rid of their boat. For $400 each, Max could make us Massachusetts boat people. Having double that in my bank account, I signed a check, sight unseen. And when I finally got to meet our boat down at the harbor, it felt like we had gotten away with larceny.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I wish you could have seen it, a 1950s Hiliner, a glamorous little wooden motorboat with an engine hanging off the back, polished wood, two rows of white vinyl seats, chrome finishes. Think Italian vacation, like The Talented Mr Ripley, but right here on the Boston Riviera. Also, like Boston's own Matt Damon in The Talented Mr Ripley, a new high-society life was waiting for us.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: The first time I got on the boat, it really felt like magic. We honked just the right number of times and a bridge opened up for us like a bouncer unclipping a red velvet rope to the VIP section. We entered the Charles River and stopped to admire the sailboats swirling around us.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: A small motorboat pulled up to us. The man asked if we were stranded.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: No, sir, just enjoying this beautiful day. Thanks for asking.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Well, you know, you're parked in the middle of a regatta.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: He looked us over. Do you guys work for Google?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: The plan to cosplay our way to high society was already working.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Max knew the next step. We had to announce our old boat as the newest member of Boston's watery glitterati, which meant a christening party. Max had been practicing for this moment his whole life. The man loves extravagant gestures.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: He invited friends from near and far to the Charles River Esplanade and asked everyone to wear white. He showed up in black, a rented black tuxedo. Max stood on the front of the boat, named it Marjorie, after his own mother, and smashed a purple bottle of Andre sparkling wine on the nose.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Now I don't know if you believe in curses, and we didn't know it right away, but Max invoked roughly three curses in that moment. Wearing a black tuxedo to a white party of your own design, that's more of a faux pas, not a curse. But number one, renaming a boat, that's a curse. Number two, Jews like Max don't name children after living relatives. Now, the prohibition doesn't specify boats, so let's call that a half curse. Number three, smashing champagne on a used boat-- I heard that's a curse, but only if you consider Andre sparkling wine to be champagne.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Now it's impossible to say which curse attached itself to the Marjorie. But moments later, the sky darkened and we all scattered as sheets of rain fell upon us.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: The next day, the clouds cleared. Our friends were still in town so we tried to take them out again. Now this is where the story really begins.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: It was a beautiful day. I think it was early summer and really sunny and gorgeous. And there were maybe 12-- 12 of us on the boat? Does that sound right?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Nine in a boat that was maybe made for six. But our captain, Max, had just completed a boat safety course. And he told us the only limit for boat capacity is having enough life jackets for everyone, which isn't true. But we didn't know that and Max denies ever saying it. Squished together, two in the front seat, four in the back, three others perched on the sides, we headed out.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: People are taking turns driving, which is really fun. I got to take the wheel for a little bit. And I was cutting across the waves, in a way, where we'd like catch a little bit of air and slam down and catch some air and slam down, which I thought was very fun. And then at one point, somebody leaned over and said to me, Sophie, this is a wooden lake boat.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: The Marjorie wasn't built for high-octane thrills. Someone says, we should get back soon. But Sophie overrules them. And then, just like the American munitions that rebelled British ships in these very waters-- cannonball!

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: I jump off the boat because it's a beautiful day and I like to swim. And I'm messing around and looking at the boat from the water. And when I climbed back into the boat, I climbed in on the back and I just hoisted myself up over the edge of the boat. And at the point where the most force was being pushed down on the boat, a whole grip of water just flowed right in.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: I'm like, whoa. OK.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: The back of the boat dipped below the waterline and Boston Harbor began to enter.

segments.speaker: Ben Ewan Campen
segments.text: And then, almost instantaneously, the boat was thigh deep in water.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: This is Ben Ewen Campen, a moral pillar of our group, the kind of friend your mom might ask, is Ben going to be at the party? We lived together and co-owned this boat.

segments.speaker: Ben Ewan Campen
segments.text: My memory is that it was really, really fast. Just it went from regular life, you're having fun, to all of a sudden, emergency mode.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: It's still a lovely summer day. We're still on our beautiful boat. But suddenly, I'm tearing an aluminum can in half to bail us out. Turns out, half a soda can only scoops as much water as your own cupped hands.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I look over at Sophie, the most MacGyvery of us, to see if she has a better idea.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: I saw a empty gallon, plastic water gallon. And I was like, oh, if I could tear the top off of this, then I can scoop water out really fast. But I'm wondering-- I'm like, OK, I don't have anything to cut it with. That's fine. I'll cut it with my teeth. I'll just crack a little hole. And once I get a little hole going, there'll be purchase and I can tear the whole thing open.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: And I try to bite it with my teeth and my teeth are just so weak. And my hands are so weak. And I can't-- I can't do anything. I don't think I'm feeling-- experiencing anxiety. But suddenly, it's like one of those nightmares where none of your limbs work.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Maybe the weight of nine passengers was too much. Or maybe Sophie's full-throttle aerials had split the seams. Or maybe (WHISPERING) it was a curse.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Here's what we know. We're alone. We're in a small boat. We're far from shore. The nearest land to us is Logan Airport. And that's when it begins to dawn on me. If we have to jump off this boat and swim to the closest land, we would be army crawling up the banks of a government-controlled airspace.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: Look, it's so close we can just swim to Logan. And very quickly and quietly, but quite definitively, you said, I'm not going to do that.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I'm picturing my white friends being wrapped in tinfoil blankets and fed cocoa, and me being perp walked off the tarmac by Homeland Security. Not today, government black site.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Our options are shrinking. Our bails aren't bailing. The engine's not turning. There's water, water everywhere. I think we're going to sink.

segments.speaker: Toby David
segments.text: We were sinking. We were in a sinking boat.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Toby David is visiting from Philly. A gifted speech maker, he helped christen the Marjorie just the day before. Now he reminds us he is not a good swimmer, asthmatic, and does not like cold water.

segments.speaker: Toby David
segments.text: The boat is going down and it's tilting. And we're in the middle of the water and we have no idea what to do. And I'm freaking out. I'm really fully freaking out.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: I'm not hearing much. But through the ether, Ben's voice comes through and says, is anybody else noticing that occasionally one of us will ask a question and nobody will respond?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: A silent panic falls over us. It is a moment that demands leadership, decisive action. We turn our heads to our captain, Max. He found this boat, named it after his mother, sold us on the dream. And now, like a monomaniacal Ahab in a Red Sox cap, Max denies there's any problem at all.

segments.speaker: Ben Ewan Campen
segments.text: When we were all wondering what to do, one element of it was everyone saying, should we call for help? And Max saying no. Max had this really strong instinct. Don't call for help. Don't call. I know what I'm doing.

segments.speaker: Toby David
segments.text: I think Max was trying to cover up for this massive fuck up. And so he was sort of in denial that there was a problem.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: Even up to the point where the entire back end of the boat was fully underwater, the entire motor was underwater, Max was still saying it's fine, there's no problem.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: But there are two. One, we're stranded in the water. And two, our captain has gone mad. We only know how to deal with the last one. Everyone shouts at Max. Admit it. We are in trouble. You need to call for help. But Max is sitting in the captain's seat, one hand clenched around the steering wheel and the other turning the key in the ignition, like the engine wasn't underwater. The expression "hope floats?" Not true and very dangerous.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: On one end of the spectrum of willingness to acknowledge this situation, there was Max, who was just face forward, pretending he was still driving a boat. And then at the other end of the spectrum, the other extreme, was there was-- there was this one wild card.

segments.speaker: Toby David
segments.text: Cath-- oh, my god. I don't know anything about her.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: She just sort of appeared in a beam of clarity.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Cath Spangler went to college with Max. She is the ninth passenger and the one outsider. When Max invited her on a ride, he had not mentioned there would be so many of us. For most of the trip, she was shy and off to the side. But now the strangers surrounding her are screaming at the one person she knows. And he has lost control.

segments.speaker: Cath Spangler
segments.text: I remember, just really clearly, looking over at Max, sitting there in the captain's seat, with his eyes kind of downcast, frozen. And something-- there was a switch that flipped in me. If the boat sinks and all of us are in the harbor, we're no longer visible to anyone. We're just little heads. No one can see us. We can tread water for a while.

segments.speaker: Cath Spangler
segments.text: What if we get a cramp, get tired, swallow water? How long can we do that for? What if the current takes us out further? I didn't want to let myself go there, but I remember thinking that people were going to die. If we don't do something, people are going to die today.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: And in that moment, Captain Cath is born.

segments.speaker: Cath Spangler
segments.text: My mind went really blank and calm. And it was like a calculator filled my brain. And I was just very logical and I started focusing on actions. Where are the life vests? How many do you have? I took on this voice that was very bossy and direct.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Like Boston's own Matt Damon in Good Will Hunting, she begins solving the unsolvable problem. Namely, if nine passengers get in a boat which turns out to only have eight life jackets-- not one per person as we had been led to believe, Max-- and now some of those life jackets are unreachable in the underwater part of the boat, how many passengers are totally screwed?

segments.speaker: Cath Spangler
segments.text: I remember looking over and there was this guy who looked really pale. He just didn't look like he was doing very well. And I asked him-- I said, can you swim well? And he said, no, I can't. And I just gave him the life vest. I took it off my neck, put it on his, and said, well, I can.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Cath hands out the remaining life jackets based on need. The water is rising. We are coming apart and preparing to abandon ship.

segments.speaker: Cath Spangler
segments.text: And that's when I got on top of the bow of the boat.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: She climbs to the front of the boat and starts waving her arms to the pilots in airplanes over our heads, to nearby boats in the water, anyone who might be able to come to our rescue.

segments.speaker: Ben Ewan Campen
segments.text: She was the one person who was like, what the fuck is wrong with you people? Of course we need help.

segments.speaker: Sophie Tintori
segments.text: And she like stood up on the boat and started waving her arms and trying to get the attention of a boat that I didn't realize was also quite close, that was, like, the rescue boat.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: An actual rescue boat just within waving distance.

segments.speaker: Cath Spangler
segments.text: It was so much taller than us, off the waterline. And there were guys on deck, kind of looking down and almost chuckling at us, making light of the situation. And I remember feeling like, they have no idea what we've been through.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: They must have radioed for a tow boat because one arrives within minutes. The captain calls down, do I have permission to perform a life rescue?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Who says no to that?

segments.speaker: Toby David
segments.text: I have to confess one thing really fast.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Toby is admirably honest about what happened next.

segments.speaker: Toby David
segments.text: I just have to say, I'm sure that, when the rescue boat arrived, that I-- I may have been the first person off of the sinking ship. I fucking levitated to that ladder to get off that boat. So that's not great for me.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: We climbed off the boat to safety. And just like Matt Damon in Saving Private Ryan, we were going home. Cath says she looks back at this moment a lot, that it's become pivotal to her understanding of herself. She's proud that she jumped in and saved us.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: It was a tragic ending for our captain. From the safety of our tow boat, I can still picture him down there, alone on the Marjorie, refusing to abandon ship. And that was the last time I ever saw him. He died that day.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Yeah, the only honorable thing I could have done. I went down with the ship.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Captain Max died. My friend Max survived. A little bruised-- his ego and his reputation for big schemes with little consequences. And while the boat became the story Sophie likes to tell more than any other, not Max.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: This is a story I have told the least. I can't overstate to you how big a failure this was, one of the most embarrassing failures of my entire life. It's a thing I look back at and shudder.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Max spent more than a decade feeling terrible. The rest of us spent that same amount of time wondering why our friend Max was trying to gaslight us and sink us. But we'd never talked about it. None of us have. And when Max and I catch up for this story, it becomes clear that he has a completely different memory of how it all went down. He says he actually did the one thing we were begging him to do.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: I remember a lot of things. I remember calling Sea Tow and telling them where we were. I remember that--

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Wait, can I just back up one sec?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Go ahead.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Did you just say you called Sea Tow?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sea Tow is boat AAA, the boat that performed the life rescue. Max says he called them on his phone way back when the engine first stalled out. That's the reason we got saved that day.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Yeah. I don't think I made a big deal about calling Sea Tow.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: No. I didn't believe him. I just interviewed five of our friends who had no memory of this at all. So I followed up with Sea Tow. Turns out they keep meticulous records. And there it was, a call for a tow, July 17, 2010, charged to our membership under Max's name. It cost $50. Help was on the way. I guess in the chaos, Max just forgot to tell everybody on the boat.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Look, I-- clearly, I owe them an explanation. But a lot of our passive-aggressive-ass friends have never brought up this day with me.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Our story had hardened over a decade, but was built on a lie. Max had kind of done the right thing. And Cath wasn't the one who saved us. The sadistic editors at This American Life made me invite Cath back to share our findings.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Max called for help. And apparently he was the one who got help to arrive, not you, waving.

segments.speaker: Cath Spangler
segments.text: That just feels impossible.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: But I think it's true. And I'm so sorry that's the way that it happened.

segments.speaker: Cath Spangler
segments.text: I'm just completely confused. So this whole time, he has been the hero of this story but no one has known it? It's so perfect that this is the finding. It's so unlike Max, too, to not claim that, claim the credit of it and say, no, I did that.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: The final curse on the Marjorie had the longest fuse and a devastating payload. It added an asterisk to a heroic deed and turned a failed captain into a guy who kind of did the right thing, but was really confusing about it. Please heed this precautionary tale. Beware of curses. Don't try to be a Massachusetts boat person for just $400. And if you already called Sea Tow, tell your friends.

segments.speaker: Samson The Truest
segments.text: (SINGING) Well, gather round and hear this tale, all you sons and daughters, of a cursed motor boat at the bottom of the Boston Harbor. Captain Max sold them on a dream of heading out to sea, you see. They emptied out their bank accounts and bought the Marjorie-re. Marjorie, Marjorie. They emptied out their bank accounts and bought the Marjorie.

segments.speaker: Samson The Truest
segments.text: Well, Captain Max was standing proud on that fateful morning, torso bare and the wind in his hair. Suddenly, without warning, the engine died, the children cried, and the ship filled up with water. Captain Max said, I'll see you all at the bottom of the Boston Harbor, in Davy Jones's locker.

segments.speaker: Samson The Truest
segments.text: He said he'd never call for help, but did he anyhow? Or was it Cath that waved them down? We'll never find out now. Loose lips can sink this ship. Secrets never travel. Captain Max in his watery grave, how do you like them apples? Marjorie, Marjorie. Captain Max went down with his ship. How do you like them apples?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So that story was by Ike Sriskandarajah. The sea shanty was written for us by Sam Geller, who was there that fateful day. He is Captain Max's brother. He performs as Samson the Truest. Other writers in the song, Aeriel East, Chances with Wolves, and Glasser. Gordon Minette played the accordion.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, ship gets a new captain who immediately throws half the crew overboard, he says, to save the ship from sinking. We hear an insider's true, real-life account. That's in a minute, from Chicago Public Radio, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program, What I Was Thinking as We Were Sinking. We have stories today about what goes through your head in the middle of calamities, big and small, and what those thoughts tell us. We have arrived at Act 2 of our program. Act 2, "Going Down With the Censorship."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So the SS Marjorie cost our producer Ike and his friends about $400 each. The ship we're going to talk about next is significantly more expensive by $44 billion. That's what Elon Musk paid for Twitter back in October. The company has been sort of famously foundering in the water since then.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And some of the most revealing details about what it has been like on the inside at that company, among the people who work there, have come from reporter Casey Newton and his colleague, Zoe Schiffer. They make the newsletter, Platformer. They've had so many scoops.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Casey also co-hosts a podcast called Hard Fork that The New York Times puts out about the tech industry that, can I say, I love. Highest recommendation. But to get back to our story, there's been one person in particular at Twitter that Casey has been wanting to talk to, a very senior employee at the company who, while just doing his job, ended up having to take on two of the most powerful people on the internet and in the world. Those two people-- Elon Musk and the former President of the United States, Donald Trump.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Casey wanted to hear all about that, and also what it was like for the guy, what he was thinking, what he was doing, once Elon took over and the place started taking on water. Here's Casey Newton.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Yoel Roth did a lot of jobs at Twitter over the years, but it was always the same kind of job. He was in the content moderation business, one of those people who decides which of your posts can stay up on the internet and which ones need to come down. And he got his first glimpse at what life as a content moderator would be like while he was in college, on a date. He's gay. So am I.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I went out for drinks with somebody without knowing where he worked. And he volunteered that he actually worked for the parent company of the website Manhunt, which was one of the early gay websites that was very specifically sexually focused.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: And even in these early days of the web, there was already a team of people who were deciding what you could and couldn't post there.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: They had a set of convoluted rules about what types of nudity you were allowed to show in which places. So nudity, fine, but not all nudity. So there were specifics. And he described to me a system of color-coding images, of red, yellow, green, and then a team of people who were responsible for making those designations.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: And I'll never forget. He said, the people doing these reviews are almost entirely straight women. And I was just floored in that moment of thinking, God, there's a team of heterosexual women who have to look at the depraved things that gay men are posting on the internet? I'm so sorry. And--

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Right, the senior hole pic specialist at Manhunt was some poor woman.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: That's not an exaggeration.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Yeah, We hope she's doing OK. Are you out there? Call into This American Life.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I'm so sorry.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: I'm sorry for what you saw.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: After the date, Yoel had one thought.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I was like, aha, that's my dissertation topic.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Yoel was in grad school. He got his PhD and, soon after, a job at Twitter. They gave him a small desk. This was 2015. The office's most striking feature was probably--

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: A giant, life-sized, cardboard cutout of Justin Bieber sat directly behind my desk.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: Justin Bieber obviously being a major figure in early Twitter.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Maybe the most popular user, at least for some period of time.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: Yes. There were rumors that Twitter had entire servers just dedicated to serving Justin Bieber-related traffic.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Besides Bieber, what Twitter was really known for back then was its trolls. The site was plagued by users harassing other users, particularly women. That year, I co-reported a story about how the site's then-CEO, Dick Costolo, wrote a memo saying, quote, "We suck at dealing with abuse and trolls on the platform and we've sucked at it for years."

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: That was the backdrop for Yoel's new job. As an intern at Twitter the previous year, he spent part of his time moderating content. He'd seen this video of a dog getting abused. He removed it from the site, but for years, it haunted him.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: It was never even like the specific image. I couldn't-- I couldn't tell you what the dog looked like or what the video was. I just remember its existence. And I remember that feeling of seeing it and then of clicking-- I think the button said "No."

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: More than anyone ever talks about, it's this mostly invisible job of content moderation that makes Twitter usable for the average person. It's what makes every forum on the internet usable at all. And Yoel was good at the job. He got promotion after promotion in his department, what Twitter and a lot of other tech companies now call Trust and Safety. It's a hard job. And it just kept getting more complicated.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: The way Yoel tells it, there was a wild new case to examine almost every day-- foreign governments impersonating their enemies, real people organizing harassment campaigns, impossible debates over what should count as hate speech, and regular meetings over whether to put labels on tweets that didn't quite violate the company's rules but would benefit from more context, like about COVID.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: In 2020, the biggest case yet landed on Yoel's desk. It was a case about a user who kept causing problems. And this guy's fans were even more rabid than Justin Bieber's. It was the President of the United States, Donald Trump.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: This is a couple of months into the pandemic. Trump had tweeted that mail-in ballots in that year's election were going to lead to widespread fraud. And just to lay my own cards on the table, I thought that was really bad because they won't lead to widespread fraud.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Anyway, Twitter's policies prohibited misleading people about the voting process the way Trump was doing. But the company had never taken action against the president's tweets before. Yoel had to decide what to do.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I didn't see a basis for changing the policy, modifying it, winking at it, squinting and finding a violation-- there was no way around it. It was clearly a violation of our policy.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: Truthfully, there was a lot of nervousness about crossing this line-- for the first time, taking action on a tweet from the President of the United States.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: The company decided that instead of removing the president's post, it would put a label under it, a label that just said, "Get the facts about mail-in ballots," with a link to a page that pushed back on Trump's claims.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: At a certain point, when it became clear that yes, this was going to happen, it became a question of who could push the button.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: On some level, we probably understand that, in a moment like this, someone has to take a physical action to type the words, "Get the facts about mail-in ballots" and click the button to attach the label to the post. I've talked to dozens of content moderators over the years, but I've never talked to someone who had moderated the president of the United States.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: When it came time to take action, only a handful of people at Twitter had the power to do it. The company had locked down access after an incident where a former contractor, on his last day working there, briefly deactivated Trump's account. Shout out to Bhatiyar Duysak, who says it was an accident. Also Twitter had just introduced this idea of putting labels on misinformation a couple of weeks before.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: And so it was this perfect storm where it required elevated access and knowledge of this incredibly convoluted system for applying these labels. And I was the only one who knew how to do it. And so I got an instruction from my boss that said, all right, we're going to do this.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Also, because this is how life goes, Yoel and his husband were moving houses the day all this happened.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I excused myself from wrangling the dog and the movers and the relocation of stuff, and sat in the front seat of the car with my cell phone tethered to my work laptop. I was on a video call with some of the other leaders at the company who were making this decision. And I remember a countdown where I was going to push the button that would apply the label to this tweet.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: At that same moment, Twitter's communications staff was going to announce the decision.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: And it felt very important, in that moment, for the timing to be exactly joined up for some reason. We counted down. I clicked the button. And then I refreshed the public view of the tweet and saw the label. And the Communications team said, we've got it from here. And I said, OK, I have to go back and deal with the movers now. And I hung up the call and I closed my laptop. And I crossed the street, back into my apartment.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: If they made a movie about Trump and Twitter, you can imagine how they'd shoot this scene, with the Twitter employees hunched over a console in a control room, high-fiving. But in reality, of course, it's the opposite. Most content moderators try really hard not to bring their own political beliefs into the job. In a way, the legitimacy of the whole company they work for depends on it.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Shortly before that Trump tweet, Twitter had explained its reasoning for adding labels to misleading information with a blog post. Importantly, the post was signed with Yoel's name. But soon after that first label showed up on Trump's tweet, his name was everywhere.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I wake up one morning, the third day that my husband and I are in our new home, to my phone exploding because Kellyanne Conway has just talked about me on Fox News and has said that I'm responsible for the censorship of the president's account and am responsible for censorship at Twitter, more generally. And in that moment, everything exploded.

segments.speaker: Donald Trump
segments.text: Thank you very much. We're here today to defend free speech from one of the gravest dangers--

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: The president held up a copy of The New York Post, with me on it, in the Oval Office as he announced an executive order restricting censorship by Silicon Valley companies.

segments.speaker: Donald Trump
segments.text: His name is Yoel Roth. And he's the one that said that mail-in balloting-- you look-- mail-in-- no fraud. No fraud, really?

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: And for weeks, discussion of me and my political opinions and my beliefs became a symbol of everything that was allegedly wrong with Silicon Valley and with the decisions that companies have made.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Twitter had to hire security to protect Yoel and his husband. It had all taken him by surprise. He'd expected the criticism, but not that he would be the target. In cases like this, people would usually come after the CEO or the company itself. But soon, Yoel realized that what his harassers were doing was much more effective.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: If you make companies believe that their employees could be hurt for enforcing the rules, they might be more reluctant to enforce them. Twitter didn't stop though. They kept putting labels on his tweets. And Trump, of course, lost the election-- though that's probably not how he would describe what happened. And after the January 6 attacks at the Capitol, he lost his Twitter account too. Yoel did not press the button on that one, but here's a detail about that day that I love.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: Yeah, there was a technical question about whether it would work or whether Twitter would crash.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Can you actually ban Donald Trump's account--

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: Banning somebody with that many followers is actually technically very complicated. When you suspend somebody, Twitter systems have to figure out what to do with all of the people who followed them. And--

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: In other words, if you follow Trump, Twitter has to remove him from your list of follows.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: Which sounds very straightforward. But when you have to do that tens of millions of times, immediately-- we had to think about, if we push this button, is the site going to go down?

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: As it turned out, the site stayed up and Trump was banned-- for a while anyway. It was such a strange moment. With the click of a mouse, Twitter had managed to do something that Congress attempted twice and failed-- to punish Donald Trump in a way that had real and immediate consequences for him.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Trump headed off to Mar-a-Lago. Yoel got promoted. He was running the whole department. And that's when another mouthy rich guy started to complain about all the rules on Twitter. That guy was Elon Musk.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: In April 2022, Musk announced he'd acquired a big stake in the company. A few days after that, he announced his intention to buy it outright. As soon as the news broke, Yoel's employees started asking what it meant for them. Elon had been tweeting a lot about free speech and his feeling that Twitter didn't have enough of it.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: He posted a photo of six people in dark robes with the caption, "shadow ban council reviewing tweet" and "Truth Social exists because Twitter censored free speech." Also stuff like, "Next, I'm going to buy Coca-Cola and put the cocaine back in," and "Let's make Twitter maximum fun."

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Some employees working in Trust and Safety worried that "maximum fun" might mean Elon would dismantle their whole operation. Yoel was willing to give him a chance though.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: What I told them and what I sincerely believed was, it's too soon to tell.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: People are frequently caricatured and villainized in the media. Certainly, I was. And that's not a reflection of who they actually are. And so don't prejudge.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: At the same time, Yoel knew that his more concerned employees might be right, that he was aboard a ship that might be about to sink. He knew he needed to be alert for the signs. His solution was to make a list, to write down the red lines that he would not cross, no matter what. Most days, his job was to enforce other people's rules. But with Elon coming in, he wanted to write down some rules for himself.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: You have to have written policies and procedures so that when the moment comes to make that decision, you just follow the procedure that you had laid out before.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Your whole job was about trying to not make decisions out of impulse and emotion, but by following a playbook. And that meant that before Elon took over, you actually had to give yourself a playbook.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: That's right.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: And so on a notepad by his desk, at his house, he wrote down his red lines. "I will not break the law." "I will not lie for him." "I will not undermine the integrity of an election." By the way, if you ever find yourself making a list like this, your job is insane. Then Yoel wrote down one more rule.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: This was a big one. "I will not take arbitrary or unilateral content-moderation action." And--

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: So if Elon came up to you just said, ban this person, you weren't going to do that?

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: That was the limit.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Did people on your team show you the lists that they were making too, or talk to you about them?

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: We did.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Yoel's list of rules got its first test pretty quickly, on the day Elon officially took over Twitter. It was the end of October. Lawyers were finalizing paperwork. And Twitter staff was attempting to enjoy the annual company Halloween party. The scene was surreal.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Were you there for the Halloween party?

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I was.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Were you dressed up?

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I was not.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Lots of people did dress up though. Employees brought their kids. There were balloons and face painting. I've talked to so many people who went to this party. And every one of them has added some bizarre new detail. Some people saw a guy dressed as a scarecrow walking around with what appeared to be a handler. They wondered if it was Musk. It turned out to be a hired performer.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: As the Halloween party had started, I was sitting in a conference room doing some work. And we start hearing rumors that not only has the deal closed, but also the company's executives have been fired. And at first, it's unconfirmed.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I get texts from a couple of reporters who asked me, is it true that Vijaya has been fired? And I said, no, I just saw her. She's still online in the company's Slack and Gmail. She's-- of course not. Your sources are lying to you. And then it was true.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Such an important lesson-- always trust the reporters. Pretty soon afterward, Yoel gets summoned over to the part of headquarters where Elon and his team had set up shop. He was nervous.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: And I thought, OK, I'm about to be fired. So I walk past a number of my employees. And I don't let on that any of this is happening because I don't want to panic them, because they're there with their kids. And so I smile and make jokes about Halloween costumes and walk over to this other part of the office, where somebody who I gather works for Elon Musk in some capacity, but they don't introduce themselves. They just say, how do I get access to Twitter's internal content moderation systems?

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: And I pause and blink and say, you don't. That's not going to happen. I explained that Twitter is operating under an FTC consent decree, that access to internal systems is regarded as highly sensitive, and that there are both legal and policy reasons why we simply couldn't grant access to somebody.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Elon's aide explains that they're worried about an insider threat, someone who might try to sabotage the site on their way out. Yoel tells them, sure, I can help with that. He explains some steps they can take to protect the company. And to Yoel's surprise, the aide says, OK, you're going to tell that to Elon. And then he leaves and comes back with Elon Musk.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: Who, at this point, I've seen on the internet, but I had not met in person. And so Elon sits down and asks, well, let me see our tools. "Our" tools-- he owns the company at this point. And so I show him his own account in Twitter's set of enforcement tools. And I explain to him what the basic capabilities are. And then I make a recommendation to him of what I think Twitter should do to prevent insider misuse of tools during the corporate transition.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Yoel also had recommendations about the midterms and the upcoming presidential election in Brazil.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: And as I start to explain some of the rationale related to the Brazilian election, Elon interrupts me and says, yes, Brazil. Bolsonaro and Lula are very dangerous. We need to protect that.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: And I was floored. I came into that conversation expecting him to fire me, and instead, he jumps ahead of me to say that he is sensitive to the risks of offline violence in the context of the Brazilian election and wants to make sure that we don't interrupt Twitter's content-moderation capabilities. It was like a dream come true.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: You're thinking, maybe I'm actually aligned with this person.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so Yoel stayed. He was surprised in a good way. On Twitter, Elon talked about the company as if it should barely have any rules at all. But in that moment, one on one, Yoel thought he might turn out to be more reasonable. Maybe spending some time inside the company would show Elon the real value of those rules, which is that, without them, you lose your users and you lose your advertisers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And Yoel felt like Elon could be sensible. One of his first requests was to restore the account of The Babylon Bee, a right-wing satire site. But Yoel explained how it had broken Twitter's rules and Elon backed off.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I found him to be funny. I found him to be reasonable. I found that he responded well to having evidence-backed recommendations be put in front of him. And I, for a moment, felt that it might be possible for Twitter's Trust and Safety work to not just continue, but also to get better.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: After that, things began to move really quickly. About a week later, Elon laid off half the staff. Suddenly, Yoel was one of the highest-ranking employees from the old Twitter who was still working at the new one. And it seemed like Elon liked him. After some trolls went after Yoel for some of his old tweets, Elon tweeted that he supported him.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: The US midterm elections took place mostly without incident, same for the election in Brazil. Elon kept pushing his teams to move faster, even as he was laying them off. At first, Yoel said that Twitter still had enough content moderators to keep the site safe. But the cuts kept coming and the work got harder and harder.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Soon, Elon unveiled his first big idea for making lots of money and recouping the $44 billion he had spent to buy the company. Yoel and his team thought it was insane. The plan-- to let anyone get a blue "verified" badge for their profile for $8 a month. The company called it Twitter Blue.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: The risks seemed obvious. People would just make new accounts to impersonate brands and politicians and other celebrities. Yoel and his team wrote a seven-page document outlining the risks. But the badges went on sale anyway. And almost immediately, impersonators started buying them and wreaking havoc.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: In maybe the most famous case, someone impersonated the drug maker Eli Lilly and said that insulin would now be free. The real Eli Lilly's stock price dropped more than 5%. It was a vivid illustration of why companies like Twitter make rules in the first place. Impersonators were suddenly all over the site.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: And so, OK, we have to ban them. But somebody has to review them. We can't just ban everyone. And so you do that with content moderators. And we had instructions to fire more of our contract content moderation staff to cut costs.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: All of this seems really self-evident to me. And I think it would have seemed self-evident even before you launched this. But what was Elon's take on this? How did he respond to you raising these concerns?

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: Do it anyway. And that was a breaking point for me.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: We reached out to Twitter for comment but didn't hear back. Reporters have sometimes gotten automated poop emojis, but I didn't even get that.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Yoel had spent a long time gaming out scenarios for what might make him leave Twitter. He made that whole list. He wouldn't break the law for Elon. He wouldn't undermine an election. But ultimately what got to him was something he didn't foresee. It wasn't on the list. It was something more personal. He knew this bizarre plan wouldn't just make people lose trust in Twitter. They would lose trust in him.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: Behind Elon Musk, I was the most prominent representative of the company, period. And I became aware that when Twitter Blue turned into the predictable hot mess that it was, that people would ask, why didn't the Trust and Safety team see this coming? Yoel, why are you so bad at your job?

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: The day after the launch, Yoel and Elon got on the phone. Elon thought the problem could be fixed if Apple would just hand over all the credit card information of the people doing the impersonations. Yoel had to explain that Apple would never do that. He also asked Elon to slow down the rollout of Blue so that they would have time to hire and train more content moderators to look for impersonators. Elon didn't understand why that would take longer than a day.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I got off that phone call and thought, I can't solve this problem. I will spend the rest of my time at this company trying to bail out a ship that might sink more slowly because I'm there, bailing it out. But I don't want to spend the rest of my life bailing out a sinking ship.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Yoel had made up his mind to leave. He called a couple of his employees to let them know.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I knew that that day, I did not want to be walked out of Twitter, after almost eight years, by corporate security. I wanted to leave on my own terms. And there was an all-hands going on at the time, Elon's first time addressing the company in person. And during that all-hands meeting, I hit send on my resignation email, put my laptop in my bag, and walked out of the building for the last time.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Did you purposefully send it when you knew he was on stage?

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: Yes, absolutely.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Mm.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I knew that it would take some time for the HR team to see it and process it, for that to get to him, for him to react to it. And in that time, I knew I wanted to be back at home and not be in the office.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Was it a long email?

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: It was one sentence.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: What was the sentence?

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: "I am no longer able to perform the responsibilities of my job and resign it as of today at 5:00 PM." I remember feeling two things. On one hand, I felt relieved. And then I also just felt deeply sad. I just wanted to get home.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: So I left Twitter's garage and was driving. And I was about halfway across the Bay Bridge when I think Zoe broke the news that I left Twitter, and my phone exploded. And I get--

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Wait. You didn't even get across the bridge before Zoe broke the news? God, I love her.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Zoe is my coworker. I am immensely proud of her, even if she did kind of mess up Yoel's plans. The car Yoel was driving that day was a Tesla, by the way. He was leasing it. He'd been trying to return it but couldn't get anyone to respond to him. Maybe they'd all been drafted to work at Twitter.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yoel laid low for a few days. He spent some time writing, and published an op-ed in The New York Times. It explained, in a very dry and principled way, why he'd left. That's when some rando account reshared something Yoel had tweeted from 2010 about relationships between adults and minors. Around that time, he'd been working on his dissertation, which called for tech companies to do more to protect minors at gay hookup sites like Grindr.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But Elon replied with a tweet, quote, "This explains a lot." Then he linked to Yoel's dissertation. Quote, "Looks like Yoel is arguing in favor of children being able to access adult internet services in his PhD thesis." Not true. But Yoel's phone exploded with abusive messages. It made the backlash to labeling a Trump tweet look minor by comparison.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: Hundreds of messages per hour, homophobic, anti-Semitic, and also violent, just deeply, endlessly violent. And he only had to tweet once. He didn't even have to say directly, Yoel is a pedophile. He just had to wink and nod in that direction. And people took his lead.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: When Yoel had first used the internet, it felt like a small, self-contained space, separate from what we used to call real life. But by the time Yoel quit Twitter, the distinction between online and off had collapsed. And it had collapsed, in large part, because of the company he worked at, Twitter.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: The site brought together so many of the world's most influential people and then pitted them against each other in these all-consuming daily battles. And the anger coming out of that could drive people to do things, violent things. Pretty soon, Yoel and his husband were overwhelmed with death threats.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: My husband turned to me one day and said, I've seen you through a lot of being targeted and being harassed. I've never seen you look scared before. And that was the moment that we decided to leave our home.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: And so once again, they moved. I met with Yoel at the temporary house that he and his husband are staying at while they look for a new place. After all this, I thought Yoel might want a different kind of job. I would have wanted a different kind of job. The internet had almost killed him, or threatened to anyway. But still, somehow, he's optimistic about what the internet could be in a way you almost never hear anymore.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I love the internet. I really do. I think-- the internet's power to bring people together and help folks all over the world find connections that matter to them is magical and is one of humanity's greatest achievements.

segments.speaker: Yoel Roth
segments.text: I also think the internet can be incredibly dangerous and scary. And the work of Trust and Safety is trying to push that back a little bit and to make the internet more of what it can be and less of the dangers of what it could turn into.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Yoel's idealism about the internet feels radical, given how destabilizing it's been, how destabilizing Twitter has been. But I know what he means. Back when he was a teenager, the internet gave Yoel a place to discover other gay people, the chance to talk to everyone in the world instantaneously. It gave him a career. It gave me all those things too. I remember life before the internet. It was a less frantic time. But it was also a lonelier one.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Here's how Twitter is doing since Yoel left. Hate speech is on the rise. Advertisers have fled. Banks that funded Musk's takeover have marked their investments down by more than half. Musk himself has warned repeatedly that the site might go bankrupt. I kind of hope it does. Because what's happening at Twitter right now is teaching us a lesson it's taken us way too long to learn-- that people like Yoel, they're not the enemies of free speech online. They're the ones who make it possible.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: If you get any value out of social media at all, it's in part because of them. They clean the place up, make it feel good to be there. They pull us back when we go too far. And they do censor us. And of course we hate them for it. We convince ourselves we'd do a much better job if it were us. That's what Elon thought. Look what happened.

segments.speaker: Casey Newton
segments.text: Nobody likes the guy enforcing the rules. But watching Twitter sink into the ocean, you can't help but notice how much you miss that guy when he's gone.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Casey Newton. He's the co-host of the podcast Hard Fork, from The New York Times, who are our collaborators on this. He also writes the newsletter Platformer. His story was produced by David Kestenbaum and Davis Land.

segments.speaker: Samson The Truest
segments.text: (SINGING) Listen up, children, and give your respect to this tale of a captain in another cursed wreck. Elon was his name, commandeering his game. He took over the ship, seeking only more fame. For his rockets and cars, he had tons of acclaim. But Elon wanted more and it ended in shame. Whoa, oh, oh, oh, oh, Elon wanted more and it ended in shame.

segments.speaker: Samson The Truest
